analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to cover mental health and addiction care on equal terms with medical care.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 376-47 on September 23, 2008, but the Senate never voted on this bill; substantially identical parity requirements became federal law weeks later as part of the financial rescue bill.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells employer health plans that if they cover mental health or substance use care, they cannot charge higher deductibles and copays or impose tighter visit and day limits for that care than they apply to ordinary medical and surgical care. Plans must disclose the criteria they use to decide what mental health treatment is 'medically necessary' and must explain why a claim was denied, and if a plan covers out-of-network doctors for medical care it must do the same for mental health care. Small employers are exempt, and plans that show parity would raise their total costs by more than 2% in the first year (1% after) can opt out for a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families who have employer-sponsored health insurance and need mental health or addiction treatment — tens of millions of people who previously faced higher copays, shorter treatment limits, or outright denials for that care. Treatment providers also gain a larger, fairly paying patient base.

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans from applying deductibles, copays, or coinsurance to mental health or substance use benefits that are more restrictive than what they apply to most medical and surgical benefits.
Bars separate treatment limitations — such as caps on the number of visits, days of coverage, or frequency of treatment — that apply only to mental health or substance use care.
Requires plan administrators to make available the criteria used for medical necessity decisions on mental health care and to disclose the reason for any denial of payment to the patient who asks.

Requires plans that cover out-of-network medical care to cover out-of-network mental health and substance use care on the same terms — significant because psychiatric provider networks are often far thinner than medical ones.
Directs the Comptroller General to study which mental health and addiction diagnoses insurers cover or exclude, so Congress can see whether plans skirt the requirement.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor group health plans and the health insurers that administer them, who bear the cost of equalizing mental health benefits (though plans can escape for a year by showing the cost exceeds the 2%/1% threshold). Multinational corporations also pay: a tax provision that delays a favorable interest-allocation rule and raises the U.S.-source interest percentage is included to offset the cost.

drawbacks.text: Plans can opt out of parity for a plan year if an actuary certifies it raises total costs by more than 2% the first year or 1% in later years, and the notifications to the Secretary of Health and Human Services are kept confidential — so the public cannot easily see how many plans escape.
The mandate only applies to plans that already offer mental health or substance use benefits; it does not require any plan to start covering them.
Employers with 50 or fewer employees are entirely exempt.

To pay for the benefit requirement, the bill delays the worldwide allocation of interest rule until 2013 and raises the share of interest treated as U.S.-source from 30% to 85% — a real tax increase on multinational companies and their investors.

The bill regulates only financial requirements and treatment limits; it leaves insurers room to shape which diagnoses and treatments they cover, which is why the bill itself orders a government study of coverage and exclusion patterns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and durable: equal treatment for mental health and addiction care in employer plans, which had long been the most restrictive category of coverage. The costs are modest relative to that, and the 2%/1% cost escape hatch plus the small-employer exemption blunt the compliance burden for plans that genuinely cannot absorb it — but they also mean some workers' plans can simply sit out the requirement for a year, and the confidential exemption process makes that hard to track. The tax offset shifts part of the cost onto multinational firms rather than the general treasury. On balance, a strong consumer-protection law with real but acknowledged weaknesses.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure (which requires a two-thirds supermajority and no amendments) by a vote of 376-47, but the Senate received it and never voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 — days later, however, the identical House parity language was attached to the emergency financial rescue bill (H.R. 1424), which became law on October 3, 2008.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 22, 2008, by Rep. Patrick Kennedy with 7 cosponsors (6 Democrats, 1 Republican).
The next day, the House passed it under suspension of the rules, 376-47, with 233 of 234 Democrats voting yes and 143 of 199 Republicans voting yes.
All 47 no votes came from House Republicans.
The Senate received the bill on September 23, 2008, and the record shows no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who need mental health and addiction treatment ultimately came out ahead, because the same parity requirements were enacted into law weeks later inside the financial rescue bill. For this bill's own fate, the main beneficiaries of its Senate death were the health plans that would have faced compliance costs — a delay that proved brief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mental health patients — parity became law anyway

for.name: Rep. Patrick Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the House bill on September 22, 2008, naming it for his father's ally Sen. Paul Wellstone and Sen. Pete Domenici.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.role: Chair, Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill as amended, putting it directly on the House floor the day after introduction.

against.name: 47 of 199 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the motion to suspend the rules and pass the bill; every no vote in the chamber was a Republican.

against.name: Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the House-passed bill on September 23, 2008, and took no further action before the 110th Congress ended.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed bill to the Senate floor; the parity language instead moved days later as part of the financial rescue bill.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was strongly bipartisan — 233 of 234 Democrats and 143 of 199 Republicans voted yes — but the opposition was entirely partisan: all 47 no votes came from Republicans.

industries.industry: Employer group health plans and health insurers
industries.note: The bill requires them to equalize mental health benefits, disclose denial criteria, and cover out-of-network mental health care — a genuine cost and compliance burden. But the bill only applies to plans that already offer mental health benefits, exempts small employers, and gives plans a confidential escape hatch for a year if costs rise more than 2%/1%, so insurers accepted the mandate with soft edges built in.

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: Their services become covered on the same financial terms as medical care, with far fewer arbitrary visit and day limits, expanding the pool of insured patients for psychiatric and addiction treatment.

The bill's revenue offset delays the worldwide interest allocation rule until 2013 and raises the U.S.-source interest share from 30% to 85%, increasing their U.S. tax bill to help pay for the parity mandate.
